transcript:
Meeting: Prefix Hotspots and KV Spill Behavior - Skybridge AI deep dive
Date: 2025-10-09 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes recorded
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Laura Ng (Redwood SE), Diego Ramos (Redwood Solutions Eng); Maya Thompson (Skybridge AI CTO), Jae Park (ML Platform), Owen Li (SRE), Priya Nair (Lead ML Eng)

Summary:
Short session focused on reproducing and mitigating frequent KV cache spillover observed at Skybridge under bursty inference with long prompt prefixes. Walked through runtime instrumentation, eviction heuristics, prefetch options, and a pragmatic test matrix (batch sizes, seq len, quantized model).

Topics: KV cache layout, prefix reuse vs hotspotting, eviction backpressure, paging to host, telemetry to detect prefix churn, prefetch heuristics, dedicated vs hosted routing, quantization tradeoffs for peak throughput.

Action items (captured in metadata): reproduce trace, share prefix histogram, run Redwood SE stress harness.

Transcript: 
[00:00] Samir Patel: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick context — skybridge ran into a pattern where during morning batches their inference cluster shows high token p99 and sudden spill to host, right?
[00:12] Maya Thompson: yes, that's correct. we started seeing a bunch of 2-3x latency spikes around 09:00 and 13:00 UTC. it correlates with a small set of prefixes that are super hot.
[00:23] Laura Ng: ok, got it. so we're talking about prefix-locality hotspotting, not an overall memory leak?
[00:28] Jae Park: correct. total memory sits inside expected, but the KV hit rate drops because certain prefix keys thrash the segment and cause evictions of otherwise-useful keys.
[00:36] Diego Ramos: this is a classic prefix skew problem. the runtime's KV layer currently uses an approximate LRU with segment-level buckets, so when a hot prefix blasts many unique continuation keys we get churn.
[00:48] Owen Li: side question — is the eviction synchronous blocking or async? sometimes our requests hang waiting for paging.
[00:54] Laura Ng: good question, it's a mixture. short answer: eviction bookkeeping is synchronous on the critical path and paging to host can be async, but there are backpressure points. i'll explain.

[00:59] [00:59] Laura Ng: (walkthrough) The KV is sharded by model shard + position window; we maintain a per-shard LRU sketch and an MRU/age metric per bucket. on high churn workloads the sketch misorders entries because of bursty access patterns — leading to eviction of warm prefixes. we also have a spill path that pages least recently used fragments to CPU host memory.
[01:25] Priya Nair: when it pages, do you compress the values? because our prefix values can be large for long-context traces.
[01:32] Laura Ng: currently we gzip compress pages for host spill, but decompression cost is non-trivial. compression reduces memory pressure but increases CPU on rehydrate — tradeoff depends on hit rate.
[01:40] Samir Patel: note for the record, this is why the optimize tool recommends different quantization + cache sizes per workload: compression and quantization change token generation CPU tradeoffs.

[01:48] [02:05] Maya Thompson: we pushed a configuration that increased kv_capacity by 30% and saw partial improvement, but p99 still spikes. we suspect prefix reuse is low — same opening tokens but then many unique continuations.
[02:18] Laura Ng: that pattern is the worst: high prefix reuse at short prefix length but very low reuse of continuation tokens. the runtime's prefetcher assumes stable reuse across next-token windows which leads to wasted prefetch and eviction oscillation.
[02:34] Jae Park: any quick heuristics to detect this from telemetry? we have traces and want to avoid running an expensive repro for now.
[02:40] Laura Ng: yes, three quick signals: 1) per-key access frequency distribution (heavy tail), 2) prefix life-time metric (time between first/last access), 3) complement hit-rate conditioned on prefix bucket. if life-time << eviction window, then that's hotspot churn.
[02:58] Samir Patel: we can provide a one-off script that takes your firehose and outputs the prefix histogram + lifetime buckets.

[03:05] [03:05] Diego Ramos: remediation techniques we discussed: increase capacity (obvious), change eviction policy (LRU -> seg-LFU or windowed-LRU), add per-prefix admission control (deny caching for ultra-high-cardinality continuations), and smarter prefetch/backoff.
[03:22] Priya Nair: per-prefix admission control sounds attractive — can Redwood runtime tag a prefix as non-cacheable at ingest?
[03:29] Laura Ng: yes, the runtime supports an admission bit per key; the default is to cache, but you can toggle admission via routing rules or an API. we typically recommend toggling for prefixes with >X unique continuations per hour.
[03:40] Owen Li: how do you set X? heuristics only? we want reproducible thresholds.
[03:44] Laura Ng: recommend starting with percentile rules — e.g., if a prefix is in the top 0.1% of unique continuation cardinality over a 1h window, mark non-cacheable. the Redwood console can compute that metric once telemetry is on.

[03:58] [04:10] Maya Thompson: what's the impact of switching to a frequency-based LFU variant? is it heavy on bookkeeping?
[04:16] Diego Ramos: LFU needs counters which increase memory overhead; we use approximate counting (small sketch per key) to keep overhead low. it reduces eviction of long-lived hot keys but can be slower to adapt to sudden shifting popularity. that's why a hybrid windowed-LRU/LFU works well: LFU stabilizes long-term hot keys, LRU reacts to sudden changes.
[04:38] Jae Park: we saw earlier mention of prefix reuse leading to prefetch thrash — any configurable knobs to change prefetch aggressiveness?
[04:44] Laura Ng: yes, prefetch has a tunable depth and an adaptive backoff. by default depth=4, but if prefetch-to-hit ratio drops below a threshold the backoff halves the depth. you can force disable prefetch per route too.

[04:56] [05:10] Samir Patel: let's talk about paging — when the runtime decides to spill to host, what's the heuristic and recovery path?
[05:16] Laura Ng: spill occurs when shard resident bytes exceed capacity; we choose least-valuable fragments based on age/last-access-score and stream them to host in background. recovery: on access miss, async fetch with synchronous stall until page returns; we also have a speculative rehydration path for predicted-next tokens.
[05:36] Priya Nair: speculative rehydration — is that the same as prefetch?
[05:40] Laura Ng: related but different: prefetch predicts future accesses at request time; speculative rehydration runs when we detect a pattern (e.g., session predicted to need contiguous history) and warms pages ahead of incoming requests. it's more conservative.

[05:52] [06:05] Owen Li: what's our telemetry to see stalls from host page reads? we only see p99 spikes, not reasons.
[06:10] Diego Ramos: look for request timeline where a 'page read' event is logged; we emit per-request events: KV_HIT, KV_MISS_PAGE_READ, KV_MISS_NO_PAGE, and PAGE_READ_MS. aggregate these by route and time bucket.
[06:25] Jae Park: do you have example queries we can run to produce those logs?
[06:29] Laura Ng: yes — we'll drop a log-filter command and a small replay harness in the follow-up bundle. it will produce both per-key metrics and traces.

[06:37] [06:50] Maya Thompson: another operational question — if we go to Dedicated (reserved GPU pool) will this behavior change? our concern is that host spill latency may differ on dedicated infra.
[06:58] Samir Patel: generally dedicated helps because you control instance sizing and latency to host, but the fundamental eviction/prefetch logic is the same. dedicated gives more consistent host I/O characteristics and higher total resident capacity for the same cost profile.
[07:12] Priya Nair: on-prem option — we have air-gapped deployment plans. are there differences in the KV layer for on-prem?
[07:18] Laura Ng: no architectural differences; on-prem allows custom host paging backends and possibly NVMe-backed spill with different compression settings. we've seen customers use local NVMe to lower page read ms by 3-4x vs networked host.

[07:30] [07:40] Jae Park: we also run mixed-quantized models; does quantization affect KV size?
[07:46] Diego Ramos: yes — smaller activations and KV encodings from lower-bit kernels reduce per-key memory and increase resident capacity. but quantized compute sometimes increases per-token CPU and can change latency curves; tradeoffs need per-workload runs.
[07:59] Maya Thompson: can we get a rough estimator: decrease in KV footprint for 4-bit compared to fp16?
[08:04] Laura Ng: rough rule-of-thumb: 4-bit can reduce KV memory by ~2-3x vs fp16 depending on packing and alignment; but actual depends on your library/kernel packing. we'll provide model-specific numbers in follow-up.

[08:18] [08:25] Samir Patel: let's sketch a repro path we agreed: 1) customer exports 2h traffic slice with session IDs and prefixes; 2) Redwood runs histogram + lifetime script; 3) if hotspot churn confirmed we run two stress tests: a baseline (default config) and a candidate config (admission control + depth=2 prefetch + larger kv_capacity).
[08:39] Jae Park: timeline? we need to show the difference quickly to justify Dedicated pilot.
[08:44] Samir Patel: we can run the histogram in 48 hours after you share the slice; stress tests take ~4-6 hours depending on scale, results within 24 hours.

[08:55] [09:10] Laura Ng: technical notes for repro: use sequence length 512 (to exercise long context); emulate real concurrency with 150 concurrent streams hitting 600 rps aggregate; include realistic interleaved prefixes — we will provide a replay harness. also include sampling of cold sessions to measure page-read tail.
[09:29] Priya Nair: what about eviction policy tuning values? can you propose a safe starting point?
[09:34] Laura Ng: start with windowed-LRU with window size of 5 minutes, LFU sketch decay half-life 30 minutes, and prefetch depth 2 with aggressive backoff threshold set to prefetch-hit-rate < 0.25. that setting reduces overt prefetch while preserving high-hit kernels.

[09:50] [10:05] Diego Ramos: we also suggested a per-route admission threshold: deny caching for prefixes with unique-continuation-cardinality > 200 within 1h window. that's aggressive but safe for reducing churn.
[10:18] Jae Park: can we get a dashboardable alert when eviction rate exceeds X or page-reads per minute cross Y?
[10:24] Laura Ng: yes, Redwood Console supports custom alerts. recommended: alert when PAGE_READ_MS p95 > 30ms or PAGE_READS/min > 50 for a route. we'll share recommended NRQL/PromQL queries.

[10:37] [10:50] Maya Thompson: some of our traffic uses long, templated prompts with a constant header and personalized tail. sounds like prefix reuse is high for header but low for tail — what's the canonical change?
[10:59] Diego Ramos: canonical approach: split the prompt in routing layer — treat the stable header as a cached prefix key and the personalized tail as ephemeral non-cacheable context. Redwood supports logical prefix segmentation in the request metadata so the runtime can dedupe caching.
[11:15] Priya Nair: how intrusive is that in our client code?
[11:18] Samir Patel: usually a few lines: add header/tail fields in the request JSON; we can also handle it at gateway via a rewrite. we'll share a sample patch.

[11:26] [11:40] Owen Li: what about tooling for diagnosing prefix collisions where two users share similar short prefixes causing accidental eviction?
[11:46] Laura Ng: we emit per-prefix owner histogram if you pass session owner metadata. you can correlate owner -> prefix -> eviction. that'll help decide sharding or admission by user segment.

[11:57] [12:10] Maya Thompson: Laura, you mentioned variant where we disable caching for a route entirely — will that blow up cost?
[12:18] Laura Ng: it can increase token compute cost but avoids paging overhead. cost delta depends on model and token length; we'll quantify in the pilot. often it's cheaper to compute than pay for repeated page reads if page read ms is high.

[12:28] Samir Patel: quick digression — do you have any security concerns around logging per-prefix telemetry?
[12:34] Owen Li: yes, prefixes sometimes contain PII. we need to ensure telemetry is hashed or tokenized.
[12:38] Laura Ng: agreed — telemetry supports one-way hashing at ingest and configurable retention. we do not store raw prompt content unless you opt-in for debugging.

[12:47] [12:59] Priya Nair: any quick wins we can test in parallel while you run the histogram?
[13:03] Laura Ng: yes: 1) reduce prefetch depth to 2 per route, 2) enable admission threshold=200 unique continuations/h for suspect routes, 3) increase kv_capacity by 20% for one shard and monitor. these are low-risk config changes.

[13:20] [13:30] Diego Ramos: note — if you need a guaranteed fix for pilot, we recommend Dedicated with NVMe spill and slightly bigger resident capacity + admission rules. that's the most predictable path.
[13:40] Maya Thompson: pricing question — Samir, can you give rough monthly for that config?
[13:45] Samir Patel: yes i'll follow up with a pilot pricing estimate tied to committed throughput. that's an action item.

[13:53] [14:05] Jae Park: one more technical curiosity — do you aggregate prefix metrics across shards or per-shard only? we worry about false negatives if metrics are siloed.
[14:12] Laura Ng: we do both. metrics are emitted per-shard and the console can aggregate across shards to give global top-k. for distributed events you should compare global top-k vs per-shard top-k.

[14:25] [14:40] Samir Patel: okay let's recap next steps — (1) Skybridge to share 48h traffic slice with prefixes and session metadata, (2) Redwood to run histogram + produce recommended config and repro harness, (3) low-risk toggles applied by Skybridge in staging, (4) full stress test and follow-up review.
[14:59] Maya Thompson: sounds good. we'll prioritize the slice export — I think Jae can take lead.
[15:05] Jae Park: yep i'll export and drop it in the secured S3 link by EOD 2025-10-13.
[15:12] Samir Patel: perfect. Laura, we'll assign you the SE owner for the repro.
[15:17] Laura Ng: got it. i'll assemble the harness and share the commands and dashboard queries.
[15:23] Priya Nair: thanks everyone, this was useful.
[15:26] Diego Ramos: thanks, and we'll include quantization numbers in the config pack.
[15:31] Owen Li: bye all.

End of transcript.
